claims.claim: Before submitting anything, run --batch refuses these with exit 2: -p or a positional prompt, --dry-run or --why, an unreadable or unparseable manifest (TOML for .toml, JSON otherwise), an unknown top-level key, a label outside 1-80 characters, an empty jobs list or more than 256 jobs, an unknown entry key, a wrongly typed or out-of-choice value, and defaults that name both prompt and prompt_text.
Manifest parsing: a bare JSON list is treated as jobs; relative workdir, prompt, out and codex_home paths resolve against the manifest's directory; values are type- and choice-checked per key.

Every entry is merged (entry over defaults over command-line flags), must have exactly one of prompt or prompt_text, and goes through the full single-run preparation before the first submit. If any entry fails, the call returns that entry's error code and prints 'nothing was submitted'.

Client-side checks per entry (_validate_run): --task needs --tier and the reverse; one of --task, -m, -a or -H is required; -I needs -s read-only plus -D, and an inherited managed-settings variable is refused with exit 7; -C must resolve to a directory; a workdir under /tmp or /private/tmp is refused with exit 7 unless --allow-tmp; the -o parent directory must exist (exit 2).

_prepare_submit also requires --allow-unmeasured-reserve to come with explicit -m and -a/-H and a nonblank reason of at most 2000 characters. A -p file must be openable (exit 2). prompt_text is staged into <state root>/inbox with fsync, and a staging failure is exit 1.

caller_session comes from CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID in the submitting process's environment. caller_pid comes from the CLAUDE_PID environment variable, parsed as a positive int, else None. It is not os.getppid.
SubmitArgs sets caller_session=session_id() and caller_pid=caller_pid(). So a dispatcher shell that inherited the parent's CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID submits the jobs under the parent session's id.

The daemon uses caller_pid only for workspace-write jobs with a caller_session: it resolves the pid to a (pid, boot id, start time) instance for the twin-instance check. For read-only jobs the pid is stored and never examined.

The daemon's submit runs under one global submit lock. It validates the request id, sandbox, workdir (resolve strict), /tmp (AdapterError, exit 7), prompt bytes, the -o parent directory, the main/master check for in-place writable jobs, git HEAD (writable jobs need one), model, task, tier, lane pin, provider agreement, API-key homes, and the max_attempts and max_wall_s caps.

The payload digest is SHA-256 over canonical JSON of: base64 prompt, resolved workdir, workdir git head, task, tier, pinned model, pinned lane, sandbox, sorted exclusions, resolved -o path, allow_desktop and policy hash (plus isolation, resume and reserve-reason fields when present). Name, caller session and pid, in_place, parent and batch label are not in it.

After computing the digest, submit looks up an existing job by request_id. A different digest raises ProtocolError (exit 2, 'request id already used with a different payload'). A matching digest returns {job_id, request_id, created: false} before any conflict check or file write.

A new job gets a C-1.1 job id and jobs/<id>/ with prompt.md and manifest.json, plus prompt.prepared.md for writable jobs without --no-preamble. It is inserted in state 'queued' inside the 'job.submitted' transaction, which re-checks conflicts. The daemon returns created: true.
Without --request-id each entry gets a fresh UUID4 request id, and the batch id is a separate UUID4. With --request-id ID, the batch id is ID and entry n's request id is ID-n.

With --json, each submitted entry's row is {batch, label, index, name, workdir, request_id, job_id, created, out, log, rc: 0}. out is the -o path when set, else the jobs/<id>/a1/deliverable.md hint. A refused entry's row is {..., job_id: null, rc, error, fix}. Rows are printed only after every submission has been attempted.
Exit code when every entry is submitted: 0. Inside a Claude session without --attach the mode is 'detached', so there is no inline wait and the call returns worst, which is still 0.
Detached mode is chosen when CLAUDECODE or CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID is non-empty in the environment, unless -d, SUBFLEET_RUN_DETACH, --dry-run or --why says otherwise.

Exit code when one entry is refused: the entry is recorded with its code and the rest are still submitted. worst = worst or code, so the whole call exits with the first failure's code: 7 for an AdapterError refusal, 2 for a ProtocolError such as a digest mismatch, 1 for an operational error.
Daemon refusals default to exit 7 (AdapterError) or 2 (ProtocolError). The daemon's _respond turns ValueError, TypeError and KeyError into 2 and any other exception into 1.

Exit code when the daemon is down: DaemonUnavailable during a submit ends the batch. With --json it emits the rows gathered so far, notes on stderr how many were submitted, and returns 69. If the daemon is down at the first submit, no rows are emitted.

The client refuses before connecting when daemon.lock names a provably dead process (DaemonUnavailable), and maps a missing or refused socket to DaemonUnavailable. The CLI turns that into exit 69 with the fix 'subfleet daemon start'.

The batch submit call uses the client's default 15 s timeout. A daemon that takes longer (serialized submit lock plus git calls capped at 60 s each) produces a ProtocolError with exit 1. The row is then reported as not submitted even though the daemon may still create the job.
Job states are exactly queued, running, waiting, succeeded, failed, cancelled and lost. request_id is UNIQUE in the jobs table.

A job becomes 'running' when admission reserves its attempt (the attempt.reserved transaction), before the guardian is spawned. That transaction also takes the lane-slot, out:, worktree and other leases and inserts the attempt as 'reserved'.

When no lane is chosen, or live attempts are at the limit, the job moves to 'waiting' with wait_reason 'capacity' and a next_check_at from waiting_metadata. A decision row is added only when the verdict changed (rechecks == 0).
next_check_at for a capacity wait is now + 1 s, doubling per repeated verdict to 30 s, but no later than the earliest known reset (closure until_at or reading resets_at).
Admission skips a waiting job whose next_check_at is still ahead, unless a lease was freed and the wait may be expedited. A skipped capacity wait still counts as an older waiter for its tier.

A transient workspace-preparation failure sets state 'waiting' with wait_reason 'workspace' and next_check_at 5 s doubling to 300 s, for up to caps.workspace_retry_max consecutive failures. After that, or at once for a non-transient failure, the job fails with rc 1.
A pre-launch probe that is neither OK nor limited sets the job to 'waiting' for 60 s: wait_reason 'uncertain' if the probe was quarantined, else 'capacity'.

A retryable attempt outcome (limited on an unpinned job, transient, or lost on a read-only job) puts the job back to 'waiting' with wait_reason 'capacity'. next_check_at is +60 s for transient and immediate otherwise. The notice is written only when there is no retry.

Fleet cap: admission counts live attempts (reserved, starting, running, finalizing), max_active_attempts defaulting to 4. The limit is cap - 1 when an older waiter of the same tier exists, which is the kept slot.

The scheduler adds a 'fleet' capacity block when in-flight attempts plus reserved probes reach max_active_attempts. The per-lane slot cap is max_in_flight_per_lane (2) for a lane with any fresh provider reading, else min(2, max_in_flight_unmeasured, 1) = 1.
Default caps: max_active_attempts 4, max_in_flight_per_lane 2, max_in_flight_unmeasured 1, reading_ttl_s 120, max_wall_s 21600, max_attempts 3, max_child_jobs 8.
Tier ordering: queued and waiting jobs are sorted by the policy's tier order (trivial, easy, standard, hard; a tier-less job counts as standard), then by created_at, with a stable sort.

An older unplaced job holds back a later job of the same tier only when the two compete, meaning their model sets intersect or either set is unknown. A pinned job's set is its pin; a task job's set is its chain from its tier upward.

Reasons a job sits unplaced in one pass: 'fleet-full' once saturated, 'behind-older-job', 'approval'/'uncertain', the stored hold while next_check_at is ahead, 'attempt-live', and 'workspace'. A job past max_wall_s is killed instead.

Further unplaced reasons: 'probe-pending' when the route could not be prepared (its own backed-off clock) or the chosen pair changed after a probe; dominant_rejection or 'fleet-full'/'slot-kept' when no lane is chosen or the fleet is at its cap; 'lease-held' naming the contested leases.

Lane rejection reasons: excluded, desktop, owner-v1, disabled, identity-mismatch, closed:<scope>:<until>, no-slot, below-floor and reserve:<model>:<state>. The job's label is the most common standing reason; a lane rejected only for no-slot maps to fleet-full, parent-cap or no-slot.
dominant_rejection returns fleet-full, parent-cap or no-slot when some lane is refused only for room, otherwise the most common standing reason (closures grouped as closed:<scope>), or 'no-lanes'.
For an Opus job the reserve rule applies because fable (the only default reserve model) shares Opus's provider but not its model id. A verdict state other than 'slack' adds 'reserve:fable:<state>'.

'unmeasured' means the lane has no fresh 'provider' seven_day reading with scope 'account' from source 'oauth-usage'. A rate_limit_event reading also counts if it is paired with a fable-scoped seven_day reading from the same event (same observed_at and attempt_id). It also means the lane has no active provider-reported fable closure.
A reading is 'fresh' only when its label is 'provider', its utilization is finite and non-negative, it is at most reading_ttl_s (120 s) old, and its resets_at, if any, is in the future.

The timer's usage probe reserves only an idle lane: none if the lane has any live attempt or any lane:<id>:* lease, or an auth-dead or operator-hold closure. A lane kept busy stops getting fresh oauth-usage readings and drifts into reserve:fable:unmeasured after 120 s.

What clears reserve:fable:unmeasured for an Opus job: (1) a fresh oauth-usage account seven_day reading (probe_interval_s 60) that yields slack >= min_slack 0.05 with cap_ratio 2.0; (2) an active reported provider-limit closure on the fable scope, which yields 'slack' with requires_probe; (3) --allow-unmeasured-reserve with -m and -a pinned, which records an authorization instead of a rejection. Case (1) with low slack gives reserve:fable:reserved instead.
The authorized-unmeasured and closure-slack paths both force a same-model admission probe before the work attempt (probe_required).
The Claude adapter maps the rate-limit type seven_day_overage_included to the fable model id, which is what makes a stream event's scoped reading count as the paired fable reading.

The CLI loops long polls. Each call's deadline_s is 60 (WAIT_POLL_MAX_S) or, with --timeout, max(1, min(60, int(remaining))). The socket read budget is min(deadline+15, remaining+1), so a wedged daemon still ends at --timeout.

Server side, wait caps deadline_s at WAIT_POLL_MAX_S (60) and re-reads the jobs every 0.25 s or on a change notification. It returns {jobs, timeout: false} only when every requested job is terminal and no succeeded job still holds an out: lease; otherwise {timeout: true} at the deadline or when the daemon is stopping.

Because the daemon answers only for the whole set, a multi-job wait never reports partial completions. Until every named job is terminal and exported, each poll returns {timeout: true} and the CLI's finished set stays empty.

When --timeout elapses, the CLI stops polling and emits, for every job still pending, {job_id, state: 'running', timeout: true, waited_s}. It adds exit 124 to the worst code. 'running' is hard-coded whatever the real state (queued, waiting, or already terminal but part of an unfinished set).

For a finished job, --json emits the daemon's full jobs row (every column, including state, rc, out_path, export_error, accepted_attempt_id, caller_session, request_id, payload_digest) plus 'attempt', the latest attempt row. Rows are emitted sorted by job id.

exit_for_job: cancelled gives 130, lost 125, succeeded 0. Otherwise an rc that is not an int, or is 0, maps via outcome class (auth-dead 5, cli-too-old 6) else 1. An rc in the C-17.3 table is returned as is. Any other rc maps via outcome class else 1, with a stderr note that is suppressed under --json.

The exit code over several jobs is max(...) of exit_for_job results and 124. So a lost (125) or cancelled (130) job outranks 124 even while other jobs are still pending, and a failure with rc 1 through 7 is hidden under 124.

Other wait exit codes: 2 when no ids and no --mine/--last are given, or --mine without a session id; 69 on DaemonUnavailable; the daemon's code on DaemonError (an unknown or pruned job id is ProtocolError 2); 1 on connection or read failures (ProtocolError OPERATIONAL) unless --timeout has already passed, in which case the result is 124.

A daemon restart or crash in the middle of a poll surfaces as ProtocolError ('closed the connection without a response' or 'connection failed'), which is exit 1, or as DaemonUnavailable, which is 69. Neither is 124.
The job ids passed to the daemon's wait are resolved with _job(), which raises ProtocolError 'unknown job'. A job row pruned by retention therefore turns every later wait on it into exit 2.

A wait call writes nothing to the store. The daemon's wait only reads jobs, leases and attempts and never opens a transaction, and the CLI's wait_jobs sends only 'wait' ops, so no notice is marked offered, surfaced or acknowledged.
The CLI wait loop never calls notice.ack or notice.mark. When a poll returns in under 0.2 s it backs off 0.2 x 2^n, capped at 5 s.
'wait' requests run on a dedicated 16-thread 'waiters' pool, separate from submit (workers) and other ops (requests).

_notice inserts at most one notices row per job, with session_id = the job's caller_session, state 'pending', and text '<job>: <class>; rc=<rc>; deliverable=<path|->; out=<-o|->' followed by a summary line.

For an attempt that ends without retry, the notice is written inside the same 'attempt.accepted' transaction that sets the terminal job state and accepted_attempt_id. The summary is outcome.detail plus '; unattested' or '; mismatch' when not attested.

Other terminal paths also write the notice in their terminal-state transaction: cancelling a queued job, a failed queued job or workspace failure, an attempt that never launched, and quarantine (text 'quarantined: ...').
Quarantine sets the job to lost (rc 125), or cancelled (130) if cancel was requested, and writes the notice in the same transaction. It releases only the lane-slot lease.
A failed export appends '\nexport failed: ...' to the job's notice text in the job.export_failed transaction, after the notice may already have been surfaced.
Notice states are pending, offered, acknowledged and surfaced. Columns are transport, offered_at and acknowledged_at.

notice.mark sets 'offered' or 'surfaced' (or 'acknowledged'), sets transport, and sets offered_at on first mark, for rows matching notice_id and session_id that are not already acknowledged. offered and surfaced can therefore overwrite each other.
notice.ack sets 'acknowledged' for the given notice ids whose session_id equals the supplied session_id. The only authority checked is that string.
Every notice.* op returns the session's notices in state pending or offered, plus jobless service notices. Surfaced and acknowledged rows are never returned to hooks again.

Layer 2 (PostToolUse on Bash): lists the session's unfinished jobs, narrowed to the printed job and request ids when the command ran 'subfleet run'. It takes a per-job flock under hooks/waiters/ and long-polls one job for up to timeout - 5 s (default 595 s).

When the job finishes inside the budget, the PostToolUse hook writes the pending or offered notice text for that job to stderr, or a job_summary if none remains. It marks the rows 'offered' with transport 'hook:PostToolUse' and exits 2. On timeout or error it exits 0 silently.
The hooks take their session from the payload's session_id, falling back to CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID in the environment.

Layer 3 (SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit): if the session has pending or offered notices, prints one JSON line {hookSpecificOutput: {hookEventName, additionalContext}}. additionalContext is the render_pending block (header, each notice text, then 'List: subfleet runs --mine · details: subfleet runs show <id>'). The rows are marked 'surfaced' with transport 'hook:SessionStart' or 'hook:UserPromptSubmit'. Always exit 0.
With the daemon unreachable, layer 3 reads the notices read-only, prints them, and marks nothing, so they surface again later.
SessionStart also spawns the sessions-kit wake worker (nudge) before surfacing and swallows any error.

The hook entries exist only after 'daemon install --hooks'. PostToolUse is matcher Bash with asyncRewake and timeout 600; SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit have timeout 30; there is also a PreToolUse guard.

Layer 4 (socket push), transport 'socket': it resolves the session by registry at delivery time. It skips when the session is not registered, not running, a lane session, has no inbox socket or no peer token, or the send fails. On delivery it calls mark(notice_id, 'socket'), meaning offered, never acknowledged.

No daemon path calls notify_push.offer or push_to_session. Finalization ends with the boundary hooks, the export and a condition notify, with no push. The socket layer is inert in this tree, and the 'skip while a live waiter exists' rule has no implementation.

'runs show <job>' in any form (bare, --json, --out, --err) calls _ack_notices right after the daemon's show returns. It acknowledges every notice on the job whose session_id equals the calling process's CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID and that is not already acknowledged. So any process carrying the caller's session id acknowledges the notice, including the dispatcher.
The daemon's 'show' op itself acknowledges nothing (a sessionless read). An offline 'runs show', with the daemon down, reads the store and acknowledges nothing.
Every store transaction that changes rows also inserts an events row of its kind. So each notice insert, mark and ack is accompanied by an event.

The -o path is resolved (symlinks followed) at submit, and only its parent directory must exist. The out:<path> lease is not taken at submit; it is taken at admission in the attempt.reserved transaction, with the job id as holder.

The export is written by the daemon after acceptance, not by the guardian or provider. _finalize calls _export once the job is accepted, and the control loop re-offers export:<job> each tick while the job still holds a lease.

_export_locked writes only when the job has an accepted attempt and the out:<path> lease is held by this job. It checks the deliverable's SHA-256, publishes by temp file + fsync + rename + directory fsync, records an 'export' artifact, and releases the job's and attempt's leases.
The publication primitive writes a temp file in the destination directory, fsyncs it, renames it over the target (replacing any existing file) and fsyncs the directory.

The job becomes 'succeeded' in the acceptance transaction, before the export. An export error sets export_error and leaves the job succeeded. A succeeded job counts as finished for wait only after its out: lease is released.
A non-accepted terminal outcome (failed, lost, cancelled) deletes the job's and attempt's leases, including out:, and never exports.
A retried attempt releases only its lane lease, so the out: lease stays with the job across retries.

Second job, live holder: submit refuses with exit 7 if the out:<path> lease exists at all ('output path is held by another job'), or if any non-terminal job has the same out_path ('out_path is held by a live job'). The check is repeated inside the insert transaction.
Second job, same request id: the idempotency return happens before the conflict checks, so the existing job id comes back (created: false) whatever the -o lease state.

Second job, finished holder: once the holder is terminal and its lease is released, a job with a different request id and the same -o is accepted. Its later export replaces the file. A lost or quarantined holder keeps its out: lease (quarantine drops only lane leases) until 'kill --confirm-dead' or '--force-release' deletes the job's leases.

v2 writes the -o file only for an accepted (succeeded) attempt. But no path in submit, finalize or export deletes or truncates an existing file at -o. A non-empty -o file from an earlier job or another writer can therefore sit beside a job that failed, was cancelled, or was lost.
The notice's 'out=<path>' text is committed in the acceptance transaction, before _export runs. A layer-3 hook can surface it while the file is not yet written, or never written if the export fails.

(a) Same manifest, same --request-id, jobs still live: entry n reuses ID-n, the digest matches, and the daemon returns the existing job id with created: false. No second job is made and the -o conflict check is skipped, so the row has rc 0 and the batch exits 0.
(b) After they succeeded: the same existing job ids come back with created: false. A following wait returns at once with the recorded result.
(c) After one failed: the failed job's id comes back with created: false and nothing is re-run. The idempotency lookup ignores state, so rerunning needs a new request id.

(d) After the workdir's git head moved: git_head is computed for every job, read-only ones included, and is part of the digest. The entry is refused with ProtocolError exit 2 ('request id already used with a different payload'); the other entries continue and the batch exits 2.

The digest also includes the policy hash and the prompt bytes. Editing policy.json or a -p file between replays turns every affected entry into exit 2. prompt_text is re-staged with a trailing newline normalized, so identical text gives identical bytes.
Validation runs before the idempotency lookup, client-side and in the daemon. A replay whose workdir, prompt file or -o directory no longer exists fails (exit 2) even though the job exists.

Without --request-id every replay mints fresh UUIDs, so each entry is a new job. With -o, a replay is refused with exit 7 while the first job is live or holds its lease, and after that it creates a duplicate job that overwrites the export.
Retention deletes job rows, and with them their request_id, except jobs whose notices are still pending or offered. A replay with the same --request-id after pruning creates a new job.
Retention protects from pruning only jobs whose notices are in state pending or offered.

contract_code_disagreements.what: The contract lists a best-effort socket push as the fourth delivery layer. notify_push.offer/push_to_session is never called anywhere in subfleet/, so no socket push happens.
The contract requires the push to be skipped while a live wait/--attach waiter exists and attempted afterwards. No waiter-liveness check exists, and the push itself is never invoked.

C-15.2 names 'subfleet wait' as the most reliable layer, and C-15.3 defines 'offered' as a delivery attempt with its transport recorded. A wait that delivers a result records nothing: no offered, no transport, no acknowledgement.

The contract says only an in-place entry whose checkout moved is reported as a different payload. The code puts git HEAD in the digest for every job whose workdir is in a repository, read-only ones included, so any head move makes a same-request-id replay exit 2.

The contract refuses an -o path held by a live job of another request id. The code also refuses whenever an out: lease row exists, including a lost or quarantined job, or a succeeded job whose export is still pending.
Exit 75 (queued, with --json and --no-wait-queue) needs result['state'] == 'queued', but the daemon's submit returns only {job_id, request_id, created} (daemon.py:829), so 75 is never produced.
The contract says wait returns 'the job's rc'. For several jobs the code returns max() over the per-job codes and 124, so 125 or 130 outranks a pending 124 and hides failures with lower codes.
The contract detects a Claude session 'by the session registry and env'. The code checks only the CLAUDECODE and CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID environment variables.

unknowns: Whether the dispatcher's Bash shell carries CLAUDE_PID, and whose pid it is. It matters only for workspace-write jobs (the twin-instance check).

Whether Claude Code runs the parent session's PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit and SessionStart hooks for a Haiku agent's Bash calls, and which session_id their payload carries. The hooks trust the payload first and fall back to the env var.
Whether 'subfleet daemon install --hooks' has been run on this machine. Without it, layers 2 and 3 do not exist and only runs show or notice.ack ends a notice.
How retention decides prune order and the 500-job / 2 GiB thresholds. retention.py was read only at the grep-matched lines.
Whether the jobs in the manifest are writable or in-place, which determines whether worktree leases and the session-instance refusals apply.
What load_policy fills in for caps missing from default_policy.json (workspace_git_timeout_s, workspace_retry_max, max_writable_per_session); policy.py was not read.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: The loop 'repeat until the exit code is not 124' stops as soon as one job is lost (125) or cancelled (130), because max() outranks 124 while other jobs are still pending.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: Parse the --json lines instead of the exit code: keep waiting on every job_id whose line has timeout: true, and treat an exit code as final only when no line has timeout: true.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: A multi-job wait shows no partial progress. Every job, including ones already finished, is emitted as state 'running', timeout: true until all of them are terminal and exported.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: Wait on one job id per call, or check real states with 'subfleet runs --json' / 'runs show --json' before trusting 'running'.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: A daemon restart during wait gives exit 1 (ProtocolError) or 69, not 124. The loop ends while the jobs survive in the store.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: Treat 1 and 69 from wait as retryable: back off, check 'subfleet daemon status', then re-issue wait on the same ids.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: The dispatcher inherits the parent's CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID. Any 'runs show' it runs acknowledges the parent's notices, so the parent's hooks never surface them. A dispatcher that only waits leaves them pending, so the parent later gets a second report of work the dispatcher already reported.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: Decide who owns delivery: either the dispatcher runs 'runs show <id> --json' for each finished job so the parent is not re-notified, or it avoids runs show (or unsets CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID) and lets the parent's hooks deliver.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: A submit that takes longer than the client's 15 s timeout is reported as not submitted (rc 1), but the daemon may still create the job.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: Always pass --request-id; on rc 1 for an entry, resubmit the same manifest with the same id, which returns created: false for jobs that were created.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: Replaying with the same --request-id after HEAD moved, policy.json changed or a prompt file was edited gives exit 2 for those entries, and a job that failed at runtime is never re-run under its old id.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: Keep the request id stable only for the duplicate-safe resubmit; to re-run a failed job, use a new id (for example ID-retry1), and treat exit 2 on replay as 'look up the existing job by request id', not as a new failure.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: A replay without --request-id duplicates every job. With -o it is either refused with exit 7 or creates a duplicate that overwrites the export.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: Always derive --request-id from a stable workflow run key.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: A non-empty -o file can predate the job. v2 never clears it, so its presence does not show that this job succeeded.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: Decide success from wait's JSON (state == 'succeeded' and export_error null), or delete or rename the -o target before submitting.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: A lost or quarantined job keeps its out: lease, so resubmitting to the same -o under a new request id exits 7 until an operator resolves it.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: On exit 7 naming the output path, check 'subfleet runs show <old job>' and use a fresh -o path rather than retrying in a loop.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: Opus jobs can wait for a long time as reserve:fable:unmeasured when their lanes stay busy, because the timer probes only idle lanes and readings go stale after 120 s. A 540 s wait loop may cycle many times with no progress.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: Between wait rounds, check 'subfleet why <job> --json' and escalate, or stop, when the hold stays reserve:fable:unmeasured.

hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.hazard: If retention prunes a finished job's row, a later wait on its id exits 2 and a replay with the same request id creates a new job.
hazards_for_dispatcher_workflow.suggested_guard: Record the results (job id, rc, out path) in the workflow's own journal as soon as wait reports them, and do not replay old manifests after long gaps.
